## Overview

Basques are a Southwestern European ethnic group characterized by the Basque language, a common culture, and shared genetic ancestry associated with the ancient Vascones and Aquitanians. They are indigenous to, and primarily inhabit, the area traditionally known as *Euskal Herria*, or the Basque Country, around the western end of the Pyrenees on the coast of the Bay of Biscay, across north-central Spain and south-western France. The Basque region includes the Basque Autonomous Community and Navarre in Spain, together with the Basque Country Agglomeration Community in the département of Pyrénées Atlantiques, France. The Basque Autonomous Community has 2,123,000 people, Navarre has 601,000, and about a quarter of a million people live in the French Basque Country. The Basque language is a genetic language isolate in contrast with the Indo-European languages.

## Material culture

### Architecture

Basque homes include the *etxe(a)*, meaning “house, home,” especially when referring to a traditional self-sufficient, family-run farm or *baserri(a)*. The home is associated with family roots, and Basque surnames were sometimes adapted from old *baserri* or habitation names. Examples include *Bengoetxea*, “the house of further down”; *Goikoetxea*, “the house above”; *Landaburu*, “top of the field”; *Errekondo*, “next to the stream”; *Elizalde*, “by the church”; *Mendizabal*, “wide hill”; *Usetxe*, “house of birds”; *Ibarretxe*, “house in the valley”; and *Etxeberria*, “the new house.”

## Music & performance

 They state only that *Bambuco*, a Colombian folk music, has Basque roots.

## Festivals & rituals

 They state that Elko, Nevada, sponsors an annual Basque festival celebrating the dance, cuisine, and cultures of Basque peoples of Spanish, French, and Mexican nationalities who arrived in Nevada since the late 19th century. The sources also state that two annual Basque festivals in Chino, California, celebrate the dance, cuisine, and culture of the peoples represented there. The Basque Museum and Cultural Center in Boise, Idaho, hosts an annual Basque festival and a festival for the Basque diaspora every five years.

## Foodways

Basque cuisine is described as being at the heart of Basque culture and as influenced by neighboring communities and produce from the sea and the land. They state that Basque restaurants form part of Basque community life in Bakersfield, California, including Noriega’s, which won the 2011 James Beard Foundation America’s Classic Award. The sources also associate Basque festivals in Elko and Chino with cuisine.

## Oral tradition & literature

 They state that some women in the past participated in collective magical ceremonies and were key participants in a rich folklore that is today largely forgotten. The sources also mention the Spanish book *Compendio Historial*, written in 1571 by the Basque writer Esteban de Garibay, which records the name of the Basque language as *enusquera*. They note that this may have been a writing mistake.

## Language & religion

The identifying language of the Basques is called Basque or *Euskara*. Basques call themselves *euskaldunak*, singular *euskaldun*, a term formed from *euskal-* (“Basque (language)”) and *-dun* (“one who has”); *euskaldun* literally means “a Basque-speaker.” The country is called *Euskal Herria*, literally “Country of the Basque Language.” The sources state that Basque is probably a genetic language isolate and has probably been spoken continuously in and around its present territorial location for longer than most other modern European languages. It is a written and printed modern language used in publication, communication, and a wide range of social and cultural contexts.

Not all Basques are Basque-speakers. The neologism *euskotar*, plural *euskotarrak*, was coined in the 19th century for a Basque person whether Basque-speaking or not. Spanish or French is typically the first language of many Basques, and essentially all Basque speakers are bilingual on both sides of the border. About 33 percent of the population in the Basque Autonomous Community speaks Basque. They mention a 19th-century proposal by Sabino Arana that *euzko* derived from *eguzkiko*, “of the sun,” in connection with an assumed original solar religion.
